261.event_title: The Doukhobors burn their weapons and bear persecution without resistance
261.place: Transcaucasus, Russian Empire (now Georgia, Azerbaijan and Turkey), and Saskatchewan, Canada
261.event: In 1895 thousands of Doukhobors, a Russian Christian sect committed to pacifism, piled up their own weapons in their villages in the Transcaucasus and burned them, refusing to bear arms or do military service. The Russian authorities responded with renewed persecution, and the Doukhobors did not take up arms in return. With help from Leo Tolstoy and from English Quakers, about 7,500 of them emigrated to Canada in 1899 and settled in what became Saskatchewan.
261.explanation: The Burning of Arms has been called one of the first mass pacifist protests of modern times, and the community chose to absorb punishment and exile rather than harm anyone.
261.tie_back: The kural defines true penance as bearing whatever suffering comes to oneself while inflicting none on others, which is exactly the two-part stance the Doukhobors took.
261._accuracy_note: A close fit to both halves of the kural's definition (endure suffering, inflict none), though the Doukhobors framed it as Christian pacifism rather than as tapas.

262.event_title: Pope Clement VI condemns the flagellant processions
262.place: Avignon, France (papal court), with the processions spreading across Germany and the Low Countries
262.event: During the Black Death, bands of flagellants travelled from town to town in Germany and neighbouring lands, performing public penance by scourging themselves in organised processions. As the movement spread and grew hostile to church authority, the University of Paris appealed to the pope. In letters dated 20 October 1349, Pope Clement VI condemned the movement and forbade the processions, and it soon dwindled into a small, hunted sect.
262.explanation: The church judged that a dramatic outward display of penance, cut loose from inner discipline and authority, had become a danger rather than a virtue.
262.tie_back: The kural warns that taking up the outward form of penance is futile for those who lack its inner quality, and the flagellant episode shows outward austerity being rejected as hollow.
262._accuracy_note: Illustrates the gap between outward penance and genuine inner quality, though the pope's stated reasons were disorder and heresy rather than the participants' lack of inner tapas.

263.event_title: Duke William of Aquitaine founds the Abbey of Cluny
263.event: William I, Duke of Aquitaine, signed a charter founding a Benedictine monastery at Cluny and endowed it with land. The charter says he gave part of his worldly goods for the benefit of his soul, and it requires the monks to pray for him, his family and others while living under the Rule of Saint Benedict. Cluny was placed under the protection of the pope, free from the duke's own control.
263.explanation: Cluny became one of the most influential monasteries in medieval Europe, and its charter shows the common arrangement in which lay patrons supported monks and counted on their prayers for their own salvation.
263.tie_back: The kural wryly asks whether people neglect their own penance because they are busy supplying the renunciants, and Cluny's founder openly paid monks to do the praying for his soul.
263._accuracy_note: A clear historical case of the lay-support-for-ascetics arrangement the kural describes, though the charter shows sincere piety and the kural's irony is an interpretation laid on it.

264.event_title: Gandhi's fast brings calm to Calcutta
264.event: When communal rioting broke out again in Calcutta soon after Independence, Gandhi began a fast on the evening of 1 September 1947, saying he would continue until the violence stopped. Within days the rioting cooled, and leaders of Hindu, Muslim, Sikh and other groups came to him pledging to prevent further violence. He broke the fast on the evening of 4 September.
264.explanation: A single old man's voluntary self-denial achieved a peace that force had not, which is why the episode is often cited as an example of the practical power of fasting and self-discipline.
264.tie_back: The kural says the power of penance, if the ascetic wills it, can subdue what opposes him and raise up those he loves, and Gandhi's fast subdued the riots and protected the people he cared for.
264._accuracy_note: A strong, demythologized example of penance producing real power over events, but Gandhi sought reconciliation rather than the destruction of enemies that the kural also mentions.

265.event_title: Charles Goodyear discovers vulcanization after years of hardship
265.event: Charles Goodyear spent years experimenting to make rubber stable in heat and cold, during which his family lived in poverty and he was jailed for debt. In 1839 he found that rubber mixed with sulfur and heated became strong and stable, the process later called vulcanization, and he patented it in 1844. Others made fortunes from the process, and Goodyear himself died in debt.
265.explanation: Goodyear's discovery transformed industry, and his story is often told as an example of single-minded persistence through hardship.
265.tie_back: The kural urges people to take up disciplined effort now because it delivers what one seeks, and Goodyear's years of privation did deliver the exact result he had been pursuing.
265._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shows endurance yielding the desired result, but it is secular perseverance rather than penance, and Goodyear gained the discovery without the wider rewards.

266.event_title: Pope Celestine V resigns the papacy for the life of a hermit
266.place: Italy (Papal States and Kingdom of Naples)
266.event: Pietro da Morrone, an elderly hermit from the Abruzzi mountains, was elected pope in July 1294 and took the name Celestine V. After about five months he issued a decree that a pope could abdicate and then resigned, because he lacked administrative skill and believed the office endangered his soul. He hoped to return to his hermitage but was held under supervision by his successor, Boniface VIII, until his death.
266.explanation: Celestine was the first pope to resign of his own free will, and he chose the life of prayer over the highest office in the Western church.
266.tie_back: The kural says those who practise penance are doing their own true work while others labour for their own ruin, and Celestine judged the busy papacy a danger and the hermit's life his real task.
266._accuracy_note: Captures the kural's inversion of values (ascetic life as the real work), though the other half, worldly striving leading to ruin, is only implied.

267.event: Convinced that his deafness was permanent and worsening, Ludwig van Beethoven wrote a long letter to his brothers at Heiligenstadt describing his despair and his isolation from others. He wrote that only his art held him back, and that he could not leave the world before producing all he felt called to create. The letter was never sent and was found among his papers after his death, and in the following years he composed works such as the Eroica Symphony.
267.explanation: The document marks the turning point at which Beethoven resolved to keep working through his affliction, and much of his greatest music came after it.
267.tie_back: The kural compares the ascetic to gold that shines brighter the more it is burned, and Beethoven's suffering was followed by the most brilliant period of his work.
267._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of suffering refining a person into greater brilliance, though Beethoven's affliction was involuntary rather than chosen penance.

268.event_title: A million mourners honour Brother André, the humble doorkeeper
268.event: Alfred Bessette, known as Brother André, was a lay brother of the Congregation of Holy Cross who served for decades as doorkeeper of the Collège Notre-Dame in Montreal, welcoming the sick and troubled who came to him. He was the driving force behind the building of Saint Joseph's Oratory on Mount Royal. When he died on 6 January 1937, more than a million people came to pay their respects, and he was canonized in 2010.
268.explanation: A man with no rank, wealth or education beyond the basics drew one of the largest outpourings of public reverence in Canadian history.
268.tie_back: The kural says the one who has let go of the sense of I and mine is worshipped by all, and a self-effacing porter was honoured by multitudes.
268._accuracy_note: A close fit for egolessness winning universal reverence; the inner state of selflessness is inferred from his humble life rather than directly documented.

269.event_title: Shackleton brings every man of the Endurance expedition home alive
269.place: Weddell Sea, Elephant Island and South Georgia, Southern Ocean
269.event: After the ship Endurance was crushed by Antarctic pack ice, Ernest Shackleton's 28 men camped on the ice and reached Elephant Island in lifeboats. Shackleton and five companions sailed the small boat James Caird about 800 miles to South Georgia, and three of them crossed the island's mountains on foot to reach the Stromness whaling station on 20 May 1916. On 30 August 1916 the Chilean tug Yelcho rescued the 22 men left on Elephant Island, and not one member of the ship's crew died.
269.explanation: The expedition became a classic example of endurance and self-discipline defeating seemingly certain death.
269.tie_back: The kural says those who gain the strength of disciplined endurance can leap even beyond Death, and Shackleton's men survived an ordeal that should have killed them.
269._accuracy_note: Next-best only: a vivid case of endurance overcoming death, but it is physical survival, not the spiritual power of tapas or liberation from death that the kural intends.

270.event_title: Ninomiya Sontoku revives impoverished villages through diligence and thrift
270.event: Ninomiya Sontoku, a farmer who had rebuilt his own family's ruined farm, was engaged to restore struggling villages and estates. He taught sincerity, diligence, living within one's means and giving back, and he preferred loans repaid from the villagers' own harvests to outright grants. The districts he developed suffered very little in the great famine of 1836, and his teachings grew into the Hotoku movement.
270.explanation: Sontoku showed that the poverty of many villages could be reversed when people adopted steady self-discipline, and he became a national model of diligence.
270.tie_back: The kural says so many are destitute because few practise disciplined effort, and Sontoku's work turned poor villages around by teaching exactly that discipline.
270._accuracy_note: A good fit for the economic reading of the kural (discipline as the cure for want), though Sontoku's discipline was practical frugality rather than religious penance.
